entry.title: The Secret History Of Dodger Stadium’s Mysterious Concrete Murals
entry.summary: L.A. Material is an independent news organization aimed at filling some holes in the Los Angeles news landscape and making that fascinating, fragmented city more legible. You can learn more, and subscribe, at lamaterial.com. This story originally ran at the site on Sept. 30. I had been going to Dodger Stadium with my dad for about 30 years before he pointed them out to me. “See that?” he asked, gesturing toward two rectangular panels of concrete on a far wall of the main seating structure. They looked almost like friezes, carved with inscrutable designs. My dad had been wondering about them for decades. Turns out the pieces he’d spotted are just the beginning. Eventually I’d locate more custom bas-relief sculptures around the park—about a dozen in total. Smaller ones visible from the field-level entrances. Massive, multi-story pieces that wrap around certain outside corners of the building. They’re subtle: abstract scenes unadorned with color, camouflaged into the rest of their concrete environments, in some cases obscured by trees and bushes.

entry.title: It’s Jake Bauerses All The Way Down
entry.summary: After a flyout and a strikeout in his first two attempts, Jake Bauers's third time facing Blake Snell in Wednesday's Game 3 of the National League Championship Series went like this: Bauers took a slider down the middle of the plate for strike one. He took two non-competitive pitches down low to make the count 2-1. He foul-tipped a changeup, and then, sitting on two strikes, four pitches into his at-bat, he decided that he simply would not strike out again. So Bauers fouled off a slider in the zone, then a curveball. He laid off an inside fastball to draw the count full. Then he managed to foul off a high fastball, and, immediately after, slowed down to catch a changeup in the zone. As the pitch count for this at-bat ticked over into double digits, Bauers pulled a slider that sat up in the zone a bit too much, sending it into the stands past the right-field foul pole. On the 11th pitch, Bauers made no mistake. Snell threw a middle-middle, 98-mph fastball, and Bauers smoked a no-doubt, two-run homer that carried over 400 feet into right field to give the Milwaukee Brewers a 3-2 lead. When Bauers's teammate Garrett Mitchell hit his own home run off Snell just two pitches later, it was, comparatively, an anticlimax. Spiritually speaking, a guy hitting a home run one pitch after just missing out on another home run counts for two home runs. Bauers had already won the game; Mitchell's own homer was just overkill on Snell's way out.

entry.title: Michael Porter Jr. Again Stands Athwart History, Saying “Damn, That’s Crazy”
entry.summary: It is late August, the waning days of a long summer. Though the oppressive heat still imposes itself on you, the days are shortening noticeably, the faint whisper of a chill in the air perceptible in the stiller moments of deep night. Soon there will be red leaves, sweaters onto shoulders, and NBA basketball. You both anticipate and fear the turnover of the seasons, though it feels abstract—that is, until your phone lights up. Someone has sent you an Instagram link to a clip from Michael Porter Jr.'s podcast, Curious Mike, where he and Lonzo Ball are inadvertently inventing effective altruism from first principles. Unable to look away, you scroll further and select a clip with the banner text "HOW WOMEN ARE TOXIC," and the captioned text "girls be toxic," learning about how these females often display toxic tendencies. Ah yes, you think to yourself, Brooklyn Nets basketball is right around the corner. Porter Jr. is a figure of fascination around these parts, as he is a starting-caliber NBA player who is seemingly more dedicated to cutting odious podcast clips than he is to helping his team win basketball games. Last offseason, Porter Jr. called attention to himself—it wouldn't be quite right to say he "got himself in trouble" or "generated controversy," since those formulations presuppose both a consensus reality against which he clashed, and a mechanism of consequence that doesn't exist—by going on one of the Nelk Boys' podcasts and saying stuff like, "I'm not saying I'm a misogynist or anything, but I'll throw on some Andrew Tate and see how they react," because you have to "test a girl early" and "do your research." It was an occasion to reflect on the alarming, shrinking distance between high-level athletes and the internecine culture of the right-wing internet, which is to say: the internet.

entry.title: What Makes A Good Critic?
entry.summary: Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season. Got something you wanna contribute? Email the Roo. You can also read Drew over at SFGATE, and buy Drew’s books while you’re at it. “Everyone’s a critic” has been a lament my entire life, but the advent of the internet rendered it literally true. Anyone can review anything online, from new albums to tubes of toothpaste. But just because you can review something doesn’t mean you’re doing criticism. It’s easy to conflate the two nouns, especially now that the occupation of professional critic is all but extinct. Every critic out of a job has been replaced by an endless crowd of civilian reviewers, which means fewer enlightening pieces of cultural criticism. That sucks for a lot of reasons, but above all, it leaves the culture at large unable to understand what good criticism looks like, or even what criticism is. Because criticism isn’t just me telling you “This was great” or “This sucked.” A good critic provides necessary context to whatever it is that they’re evaluating. My favorite music critic ever is Stephen Thomas Erlewine, who used to review albums for AllMusic before the site cut him loose and he was forced to open up his own Substack. Erlewine knows far, far more about music than I do. He's listened to every previous album/B-side an artist has put out before reviewing their newest release. He knows the background story of how that album was made. He knows if the lead singer and lead guitarist stopped talking to each other a week into the recording sessions. He knows the producer of the album, and he’s heard all of the other albums that producer has made. He’ll render a final judgment on a work, as the job requires, but he’s done enough homework to make certain that his is an educated judgment.

entry.title: Irreal: Saving Window Configurations
entry.summary:
techhub.social, lispwizard has a short post (or whatever techhub.social calls them) on saving window configurations to registers. He notes how easy it is to save multiple configurations and switch between them on the fly.
Saving window configurations and other data in registers is an extraordinarily powerful technique that all Emacs users should learn and master. There’s a problem, though, when you want to do this programmatically: which register should you use? How can you be sure that your choice won’t conflict with a register that the user has chosen manually for some other task? There are several situations in which I want to run an Emacs function in a single window—Elfeed is an example—and I do that by saving the current window configuration, deleting the other windows, running the required function, and then restoring the previous window configuration but how do I choose a “safe” register to save the window configuration in?
The answer is a trick I learned from Magnar Sveen years ago. Instead of using a letter to name the register, you use a symbol like :saved-windows. That works because when you name a register with a letter, Emacs uses a pointer to its symbol as the register name. Using a symbol name like :saved-windows works because the result is also a symbol pointer.
If you have the need to save something in a register programmatically, this is a good way of doing it. You don’t have to worry about conflicts because the user can not use symbol names for registers interactively.

If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it." Now, because the laws have not changed, Rooney and her publisher Faber & Faber announced this week that they will no longer be publishing her work in the U.K. Rooney's novels have sold more than 2 million copies in the U.K. alone, a monumental number for any modern novelist. Her books Normal People and Conversations with Friends have been adapted for television. In her op-ed last year, Rooney stated that she intended to give the royalties from her books sold in the U.K., as well as her residuals from the television adaptions of her novels, to Palestine Action, a direct action network known for disrupting weapon manufacturers that sell arms to Israel. Under U.K. anti-terrorism laws, Rooney's publisher can no longer give her the royalties for her novels, knowing that she will donate them to Palestine Action, without putting them both at risk. Technically, Rooney's books could still be sold in the U.K., but she would not be paid for their sales. Her publisher did not want to withhold the earnings from her. "As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber & Faber said in a statement.

quick post on Sacha’s solution to a problem posed by David Pape. I thought it was a nice solution but then 0-_-0_ pointed out that abo-abo had already solved this problem with his tiny library. So I wrote about that and prepared to move on.
I was not allowed to. Frequent commenter Phil remarked in my original post that he would use a keyboard macro. He suggested that that would make sense for those of us who who seldom need to enter a sequence of ranges like Pape. In Pape’s case this was something that he needed to do a lot so a solution like Sacha’s or abo-abo’s make sense. I agree with Phil. A keyboard macro is exactly how I would solve this problem given that I seldom have it.
This seems pretty obvious and might not be worth writing about except that Phil’s solution showed me something that I didn’t know: You can set the initial value of the counter with a Ctrl+u n where n is the desired initial value. That’s a lot easier than using Ctrl+x Ctrl+k Ctrl+c to do the job.
As a final note, I think that Phil had a typo in his macro. As far as I can tell it should be
C-u 47 <f3> # <f3> , SPC <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4> <f4>
At least that’s what works for me.
It turns out that I regularly use a macro with a counter so I’m really happy to learn that the counter can be set so easily.

entry.title: James Dyer: Org Speed Keys: Making t Land After the TODO Keyword
entry.summary:
org-use-speed-commands all the time when navigating and performing actions on org headlines, but I think I have found a friction point, something that just feels a little off.
When the point is on * and then you press the key t, it calls org-todo via org-self-insert-command. Fast, but the feel is off, the point stays on the stars, so I have to move right before I can type the headline.
The reason is in org-todo itself. It has a cursor fixup that parks point just after the keyword, but only when point is not at beginning of line. Speed keys by definition run at beginning of line (org-speed-command-activate requires (bolp)), so the fixup never fires for exactly the keys that would benefit most.
There is no custom option for it, so I added a small :after advice:
(defun my/org-todo-stop-after-keyword (&rest _) "Move point to just after TODO keyword when `org-todo' leaves it at BOL. Speed command `t' (via `org-self-insert-command') runs with point at beginning of headline, where `org-todo' skips its cursor fixup." (when (and (bolp) (org-at-heading-p)) (when (looking-at org-todo-line-regexp) (goto-char (or (match-end 2) (match-end 1))) (when (looking-at " ") (forward-char 1))))) (advice-add 'org-todo :after #'my/org-todo-stop-after-keyword)
* Test with point on * plus t becomes * TODO Test with point on Test, ready to type. Same for cycling * TODO to * DONE.
Small change, but speed keys finally feel like they finish the job instead of leaving me parked on the margin!

Je veux vous présenter ma petite expérience de la reconnaissance vocale pour dicter dans Emacs et pour les contrôler. J'utilise le modèle Orukeet pour la reconnaissance vocale parce qu'il est assez rapide et assez précis. Je l'intègre dans Emacs en utilisant mes bibliothèques sachac/whisper.el et speech-input. J'ai récemment créé des commandes vocales pour ajouter des éléments à ma liste de tâches. C'est étonnement utile parce que ça réduit la charge cognitive liée à la mémorisation des raccourcis clavier. Je vais vous montrer cela.
0:37 Ajouter des tâches
Je presse la touche zéro du pavé numérique avant et après avoir dit « Rappelle-moi demain de préparer une présentation pour Emacs Paris sur les commandes vocales. » La fonction crée une tâche dans ma boîte de réception. La tâche est planifiée pour demain. Il y a un lien vers l'enregistrement
1:09 D'autres dates
« Rappelez-moi demain de préparer une présentation pour Emacs Paris sur les commandes vocales », la capture d'écran et le contexte de tâche. Ça m'aident si j'ai été mal comprise ou si j'ai besoin de contexte. De la même manière, je peux dire « Rappelle-moi la semaine prochaine de faire la paperasse pour l'école. » « Rappelle-moi aujourd'hui de créer une vidéo sur mes commandes vocales. »
1:59 Basculer à une tâche
Je peux aussi créer une tâche et déclencher le suivi du temps (ou clock in). Par exemple, je peux dire « Commence à implémenter la génération des questions. »
2:15 Retrouver le fil de mes pensées
Si je perds le fil de mes pensées : « j'en étais où ? » Ça m'affiche les tâches récentes.
2:27 Je faisais quoi ?
« Je faisais quoi ? » Ça bascule sur la tâche actuelle. Voilà des commandes vocales pour ajouter des tâches.

entry.title: Curtis McHale: Emacs Carnival - Will we change how we interact with Emacs?
entry.summary: Will voice kill the keyboard. No. Will the way we interact with Emacs, and computers in general, change drastically? No. Star Trek has a mythical AI/computer that responds to voice commands and interacts with you to clarify or note other work that may pertain to what you wanted. Evidently the interface is so ubiquitous that Scotty talks to a mouse noting it's "quaint" to need to push it and type on a keyboard to interact with a computer. But if we watch the bridge of any Star Trek show people aren't talking the whole time. They're tapping screens to get the computer to do things for them. Theoretically the captain could tell the ship where he wants to go and let the computer do it, but he issues a command and then someone types in the needed commands to the ship so it goes in the expected direction. I work at home in a solo office space. I could talk to my computer and it would disturb no one, except me. I'd be unable to listen to music on my stereo at the same time just in case the computer couldn't understand my words versus the song. I don't think keyboards are going anywhere any time soon. They provide an unambiguous interface to your computer that doesn't disturb others. I think that those loving Emacs interactions like they use it will continue to do so as they do now because it's the most efficient way to control the Emacs interface.

entry.title: I tried to move my notes out of Emacs. I failed. Again.
entry.summary: Every so often I suffer from what I call "Emacs Fatigue". It's closely related to "Text File Fatigue". Using Emacs tends to pull one toward using it for everything, which is what I'd done. Then, I simply grow tired of staring at the same thing every day. When this happens, I "decide" to uproot my life and move my notes into something else. This time, that something else was Bear. Bear is great. It's solid, beautiful, and refreshingly simple. It syncs flawlessly (for free[1]) and runs on macOS and iOS. It's also inexpensive. It uses an SQLite database, which doesn't bother me. Databases are great at this stuff. All the "But but what if the database...?!" talk is mostly hearsay anyway. The thing that made me twitchy was that it felt like my notes were "in there". It's not the database. It's the fact that everything is in an app, and that app makes me need to use that app. This is how I'd started to feel about Emacs, but mostly due to Org mode. Bear is macOS and iOS only, which should be fine for someone like me who has "decided" to live on macOS. And yet, Linux continues to emit a low-grade hum in the back of my head that I can't ignore. If I don't want my notes in Org mode files, but I'm still drawn toward Emacs, what should I do? Denote! That's where they'd all started in the first place, but as .org not .md. I'd nearly forgotten that Denote handles Markdown files natively. One Emacs configuration change and I was back where I belong. And since Bear notes are already Markdown, all it took was an export and a (Claude Code-assisted) conversion script for file names, links, and attachments. So yes, I've done that thing where I quit using Emacs only to come crawling back later. I know better, but knowing better doesn't stop me. Maybe I'll work on a sync/bridge between Denote and Bear. That would be neat. It was pointed out that Bear isn't free, so syncing isn't free. True, but I guess meant that it's not a paid extra. ↩︎ ✍️ Reply by email

entry.title: Irreal: Inserting Number Ranges As A List
entry.summary:
very nice solution to a problem posed by David Pape: how can we enter a range of numbers as list of distinct numbers in Emacs? Pape’s specific problem was entering the numbers of error reports that a Git commit closes. Rather than entering something like
closes: 47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 70
he’d like to enter something like
closes: 47-51 70
and call an Emacs function to have it expanded into the first example.
Chua has a very nice solution that covers that case as well things like
47-51, 70
or even
5-15/2
to expand into the sequence
5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15
Most of the heavy lifting is done by the number-sequence function. The rest of the work is parsing the input string into either a single number or a range of numbers that number-sequence can work on.
Chua’s solution strikes me as an example of Emacs at its best. The problem it solves is not earth shattering. It’s simply a bit of friction in a user’s everyday workflow but Emacs easily provides a solution that makes the friction disappear. Take a look at her code. It not only shows an ingenious solution to the problem but also demonstrates the power of Emacs and Elisp to make the application of that genius simple.
